newsitem.title: UK: Dated Brent slips back, other N. Sea grades steady.
newsitem.headline: Dated Brent slips back, other N. Sea grades steady.

text.p: Wet Brent crude looked a shade softer on Thursday after a U.S. refiner bought the last cargo it required to fill a VLCC due to load around May 10 for a transatlantic trip, traders said.
The refiner paid June Brent less 25 cents a barrel for a cargo loading May 14-16 after taking an earlier May 8-10 at June less 27 cents on Wednesday.
"It's looks like they're all done now and that could remove some support from Dated (Brent)," said a trader.
A second cargo, loading May 12-24, was sold by a major oil company to a trader for June Brent less 37 cents.

June Brent shed 10 cents to $18.42 a barrel by 1137 GMT but intermonth spreads were broadly unchanged in thin talk with June/July pegged at -14/-11 cents after trade at -13 and -12 cents in late U.S. dealing.
But Brent CFDs were softer, next week's dates trading twice at June Brent -33 cents, about five cents down on Wednesday's levels.
Only one May 16-18 was due to be nominated from the paper chains on Thursday.
Other North Sea crudes were stable with holidays in most European countries keeping activity thin.
West African markets were also quiet on Thursday but traders said a May 27-29 cargo of Brass River was sold earlier this week by a European major at a premium of 53 cents to Dated Brent.

"That's a pretty good number," a trader said, adding that other Nigerian differentials were steady, with Bonny Light and Qua Iboe talked at about Dated Brent +40/+45 cents. The traders said that most of the May West African cargoes have found homes in the United States, Asia or Europe but at least three, two Qua Iboes and one Pennington, were on offer.
Traders said on Wednesday that three to four Forcados cargoes were still unsold but not offered.

One trader said that a force majeure announced recently by Shell Nigeria has caused sellers to hold back offers because there was uncertainty over the loading dates. "Peole are holding back, I think it is because of that (force majeure)...One would have thought the scheduling would have been sorted out, it should have been by now. So they may start showing them again soon," he said.
